03The voices

What workers actually told us, in their own words.

"I got my mornings back. I cook breakfast with my kids now. I would take a 25% pay cut before I'd give that up." — Priya R., software engineer, Bangalore
"I miss the spontaneous hallway conversations. The 1:1s and standups don't replace what you'd learn just by being there." — Marco D., product manager, Milan

04The timeline

How we got here. Five years of policy turbulence in five lines.

2020

Forced experiment. Most knowledge workers go remote within weeks. Productivity holds, surprisingly.

2021

"The Great Resignation". Workers vote with their feet for flexibility.

2022

RTO mandates begin. Mostly ignored or quietly walked back.

2023

Hybrid emerges as the default. Tuesday-Wednesday-Thursday becomes the unofficial week.

2025

Stabilization. The companies that built remote-first infrastructure pull ahead.

05The trade-offs

Everyone gives up something. Here's what.

What workers gain

  • 4.2 hours/week not commuting
  • Lower cost of living flexibility
  • Deeper focus blocks
  • Higher reported life satisfaction
  • More autonomy over schedule

What gets harder

  • Building trust with new teammates
  • Learning by osmosis from senior peers
  • Switching off at the end of the day
  • Visibility for promotions
  • Finding accidental friendships

The verdict

Remote isn't a perk. It's a default that companies opt out of at their peril.

Methodology: Survey of 5,427 full-time knowledge workers in 38 countries, Jan–Mar 2026.
Margin of error ±1.4% at 95% confidence. Full dataset available at beaconlabs.co/remote-2026.
